extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature: scientists, science teachers, editors/compilers of scientific works and educated lay readers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance for reviewing and compiling scientific and educational writings (text-books, year-books, pamphlets, instrument designs, letters and scientific argument). Focus on organization, accuracy, pedagogy, empirical method, and terminological precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical familiarity should precede theoretical study
rubrics_metrics.description: "That some practical familiarity with geometrical construction should precede theoretical study; and that the teaching of geometry would gain by the free introduction of easy exercises and numerical examples or illustrations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbooks should introduce hands-on construction work before abstract theory and incorporate easy exercises and numerical illustrations to support learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include exercises and numerical illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching of geometry would gain by the free introduction of easy exercises and numerical examples or illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises should cover edge cases (e.g., the case of parallel lines) and be checked so no common situations are overlooked; numerical examples help comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide space for pupil-drawn figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of blank spaces being left for figures to be drawn by pupils on the printed pages, there are now inserted between every two pages of type two sheets of admirable blank paper. The paging is continued on these blank sheets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbook layouts should include adequate, well-integrated blank pages or spaces for students to draw figures, with consistent pagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate sequencing and part-division of textbook content
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three parts in the place of two; the use of the protractor is relegated to part ii.; on p. 37 a return has been made to Euclid’s definition of parallels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange topics and parts so pedagogical progression is logical (e.g., practical tools positioned where useful), and adopt agreed definitions where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimise typographical and ordering errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Oversights noted: Should not 7 precede 6 on p. 49? p. 61, 4, where a definition is given which is wanting in the former place. In Exercise 14, p. 62, the case of parallel lines has been overlooked; and on p. 50, for 514 we get 534 nearly =.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofread carefully for numbering/order mistakes, missing definitions, misprinted numerals; such errors impede student comprehension and should be corrected in subsequent editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and suitability for target students
rubrics_metrics.description: This is characterised by his usual clearness and ability. ... presented in a clear and satisfactory manner, certainly in a form not hard to be understood by an average schoolboy who has mastered any ordinary treatise on Plane Geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether exposition, examples, and level match the intended student audience; work should engage students' geometrical imagination and be readable by average pupils for whom it is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include sufficient proofs for examination candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: A little fuller notice of these solids would fit the book to meet the requirements of candidates for the B.A. London Examination; as by a recent extension of the University scheme students are expected to be acquainted with the proofs of the properties of these figures, which are assumed in treatises on mensuration of solids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For works aimed at examination candidates, include proofs of key properties rather than merely stating them; ensure content meets current examination syllabi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures must be lettered and matched correctly with proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The figure on p. 128 is not quite correctly lettered in accordance with the proof that accompanies it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that diagrams are correctly labelled and correspond exactly to the accompanying text and proofs; mismatches confuse readers and invalidate arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherent organisation and consistent heading principles for compilations
rubrics_metrics.description: The paragraphs in this volume are arranged under a variety of headings, but on what principle the assortment is made we have failed to discover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compilations (year-books, anthologies) should follow a clear, defensible principle of arrangement so related topics are grouped logically and readers can find material predictably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use authoritative sources and trace statements to originals
rubrics_metrics.description: Very little pains appear to have been taken to go to the best authorities on each subject, or to trace statements to their original source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors/compilers must verify facts against primary or authoritative sources rather than relying on secondary or popular press; provide citations or provenance where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid duplication across categories
rubrics_metrics.description: It is surely the result of careless editing to find on the same page two descriptions of the same bone-cave in Pennsylvania, although in one instance it is described, by a slight geographical confusion, as being situated 'in Philadelphia.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent repeated accounts of the same event appearing under different headings; consolidate to avoid confusion and apparent lack of editorial control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure correct spelling of proper names and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Very familiar proper names are constantly misspelt or mis-quoted. Thus we hardly recognise Padre Secchi under the disguise of ' Seeche ;' or the admirable Genevan Society ... under the name of 'The Society of Physics and Natural History of Ginevra.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful copy-editing is required for proper names and institutional titles; mistakes undermine credibility and mislead readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not present unverified or misleading scientific statements as authoritative
rubrics_metrics.description: We will refer only to a single actual error. Canon Kingsley will be surprised to be made responsible, on the authority of our excellent contemporary the Leader, for the statement that 'lime is a metal called by chemists 'calcium;' but it is never found in that state in nature. It is found in a rocky or chalk form.' Other blunders almost as gross could be quoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid publishing factually incorrect or misleading scientific claims; verify technical claims with competent sources before inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial correspondence policy: anonymity and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: [ The Editor does not hold himself responsible for opinions expressed by his correspondents, No notice is taken of anonymous communications. ]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State and follow clear policies about letters: reject anonymous submissions and distinguish editor's voice from correspondent opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for duration when inferring forces from work or velocity
rubrics_metrics.description: From the amount of work done, or velocity generated or destroyed, nothing can be inferred with regard to the acting force, unless we take into account the length of time during which it acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In physical reasoning, do not deduce the magnitude of forces solely from observed work or velocity changes — include time scales and consider whether small forces acting long produce observed effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative / order-of-magnitude arguments with known cases (e.g., tides)
rubrics_metrics.description: The velocity of motion between the equator and the pole being probably of the same order only as tidal velocities, we may suppose the friction in the two cases to be somewhat of the same order. ... the force producing the tides is about equal to the force of gravity along a gradient of two feet between the equator and the poles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where direct measurement is lacking, compare to well-understood phenomena (tidal forces, known gradients) to estimate plausibility and relative magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical indicators for cyclones: seasonality, precursor winds, barometric fall
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. There is rarely a year without at least one cyclone passing through ... 2. The cyclone season extends over a greater part of the period during which the sun is south of the equator ... 3. They are usually preceded for a few days by strong northerly winds, During such winds we watch the barometer very carefully, as a sudden fall is a sure indication of a cyclone near at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify cyclones by their seasonal timing, precursor wind patterns, and drops in barometric pressure; maintain local barometer observations to provide early warning (e.g., 36 hours notice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect systematic observations before ascribing causation (e.g., 'rain after fire')
rubrics_metrics.description: These notes are forwarded in the hope of helping to illustrate the question of whether fires cause rain, no opinion is ventured on the subject, but this curious phenomenon should be further investigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid causal claims based on isolated anecdotes; record systematic data (wind direction and strength, local vs. distant rainfall, timing relative to fires) and investigate further before concluding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument assembly should prevent internal condensation
rubrics_metrics.description: When thermometers fitted in this manner are exposed to cold, a copious deposition of dew takes place, both on the stem and in the interior of the jacket ... I would therefore suggest to makers ... whether it would not be advisable for them to dry, I do not mean merely heat, the air in the tubes, or else enclose some water-absorbing substance, as calcium-chloride, in the tube before finally inserting the india-rubber stopper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturers of self-registering/jacketed thermometers should remove moisture from internal air (drying) or include desiccants (e.g., calcium chloride) before sealing to avoid condensation that impedes accurate readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful, repeated observation of simple phenomena is valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: To your readers it is trite and useless to remark upon the interest that attaches to the careful and continued observation of the most familiar things. ... From the contemplation of such phenomena one rises with an increasing joy, and not a little humbled at one’s own ignorance before the orderly mystery that pervades everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage patient, repeated observation of everyday phenomena (drops on water, smoke, ice in sunlight) as a legitimate and fruitful scientific practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define technical terms precisely to avoid philosophical and scientific confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: It is much to be regretted that a far greater degree of logical accuracy in the use of terms than is usually met with, does not exist amongst even the ablest writers on physics ... Force is a mutual action between the atoms or molecules of matter ... Energy ... is the power of doing work. ... The term 'Potential' applied to force or energy means inactive, but capable of being called into action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating foundational concepts (force, energy, potential, sound, light, heat) provide explicit definitions, avoid conflating distinct concepts (e.g., force vs potential energy), and ensure consistency of usage throughout argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indefinite or inconsistent language in scientific argument
rubrics_metrics.description: There is probably no term employed in physics that has been more misapplied, and in its misuse has led to greater confusion of ideas, than 'force.' ... Sound philosophy would seem to consist rather in assigning appropriate meanings, involving no inconsistency or contradiction, to terms of frequent occurrence in all works on physics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should choose precise language and stick to consistent definitions; critique of scientific doctrines often arises from sloppy terminology rather than substantive error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multi-disciplinary evidence (linguistic, archaeological, ethnographic) when evaluating migration hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence from language is discussed, and the etymology ... is accepted ... The American Esquimaux never go from their own hunting range for any distance to the inhospitable north. ... The skulls of musk oxen without their lower jaws, a proof that they had been killed by Esquimaux, are also found scattered along the same coast ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate human migration theories using combined lines of evidence — customs, language/etymology, archaeological remains (ruins, faunal remains), contemporary travel accounts — and weigh the authority of experts on the subject.
